module.title: Markets 0 — Prices, Returns & Trading Mechanics
module.destination: Read and audit a basic market record: separate price/cash flow/payoff, compute simple/gross/log/total returns, keep long/short P&L signs straight, interpret quotes/orders/fills, aggregate executions, and reconcile a small cash/position/P&L ledger without importing later microstructure or asset-pricing theory.
module.gate: Page completion is not clearance. Every owned market-mechanics capability must be publicly elicited and scored, fixed assessments must remain distinct from instruction, and evidence must preserve exposure/version provenance.
module.nextBoundary: M08 owns programming/simulation. Deep market-data engineering, microstructure, asset pricing, portfolio construction and execution optimization remain much later.

sessions.title: Price, cash flow, payoff & trade cash amount
sessions.focus: Separate the price paid now from later cash flows/payoffs and compute quantity×price cash amounts.
sessions.purpose: Prevent the foundational error that a quoted price is itself a future payoff or profit.
sessions.centralCapability: A price is an exchange amount per unit at a time; later cash flows and terminal sale proceeds are separate ledger events.
sessions.principalObstacle: Price, cash flow and profit are all money-valued, so beginners often collapse distinct ledger events into one number.
requiredOwnership: Use a quoted entry price as the per-unit input when computing trade cash amount.
Distinguish price, intermediate cash flow and terminal sale proceeds/payoff.
Compute the cash amount of a trade as quantity×price with direction stated.
Track explicit later cash flows separately from the initial trade.
Explain why the initial market price is not itself the future payoff or profit.

sessions.lesson: A market price tells you how much is exchanged per unit at a particular time. It is not the same object as a later dividend/coupon/cash distribution, a terminal sale price, or the net profit from the whole position. A buy of q units at price P uses qP of cash before fees. Worked example: Buy 2 units at 15, later receive a cash distribution of 1 per unit, then sell at 17. The initial trade cash outflow is 30, the later distribution is 2, the sale brings 34, and the net cash gain across those stated events is 6. The price 15 was neither the later distribution nor the final profit. Guided check: Buy 3 units at 8, later receive .5 per unit and sell at 9; list the three cash events before netting them.

sessions.title: Order, quote, trade, fill & signed position
sessions.focus: Build the market vocabulary needed to read a basic trading record without conflating instructions, displayed prices and executed quantity.
sessions.purpose: Later research data are meaningless if order intent, quote state, execution and inventory are treated as the same event.
sessions.centralCapability: Distinguish order, quote, trade/fill and position, and update signed inventory from an executed quantity.
sessions.principalObstacle: Submitted quantity, displayed quote, executed fill and resulting inventory can coexist in one record but describe different states.
requiredOwnership: Define an order as an instruction rather than an execution.
Define a quote as displayed market information rather than a completed trade.
Define a fill/trade as an executed quantity at an execution price.
Compute the unfilled remainder of a partially filled order.
Update a signed position from the executed quantity rather than the submitted quantity.

sessions.lesson: An order is an instruction to buy or sell. A quote is displayed market information. A fill is the part of an order that actually executes; a trade record says that quantity changed hands at a price. Position is inventory after executions, not after mere submissions. Use positive quantity for long inventory and negative for short inventory. Worked example: Start flat and submit an order to buy 10 units. Six execute at 20.1 and four remain working. The fill is 6, the unfilled remainder is 4, and position is +6—not +10. Guided check: Start at position −5, submit a buy for 8 and receive a fill for 3; update the position using only the fill.

sessions.title: Arithmetic/simple return from two prices
sessions.focus: Compute and interpret one-period simple return with denominator discipline.
sessions.purpose: Return normalizes a price change by the starting price; raw price change and percentage return are different quantities.
sessions.centralCapability: Use R=(P1−P0)/P0 for positive starting price and interpret sign/units correctly.
sessions.principalObstacle: Learners often report the currency price change as if it were already a percentage return or divide by the ending price.
requiredOwnership: Write the simple-return formula with starting price in the denominator.
Compute the absolute price change separately from the return.
Compute a positive or negative simple return exactly.
Convert the decimal return to a percentage.
Explain why a currency price change and a dimensionless percentage return are different.

sessions.lesson: For a positive starting price P0 and ending price P1, the simple price return is R=(P1−P0)/P0. The numerator is an absolute price change; dividing by the starting price makes the return dimensionless. Worked example: 50→55 gives a price change of5 and R=5/50=.10=10%. A move40→36 gives −4/40=−10%. Guided check: For90→99, compute both the 9-unit price change and the percentage return.

sessions.title: Gross return factor & wealth update
sessions.focus: Connect simple return to multiplicative growth via G=1+R=P1/P0.
sessions.purpose: Compounding later requires a factor representation rather than repeatedly adding percentages.
sessions.centralCapability: Translate among price ratio, simple return, gross-return factor and a proportional wealth update.
sessions.principalObstacle: Gross factor, simple return and P&L are often mixed even though one is a ratio, one a relative change and one a currency amount.
requiredOwnership: Compute gross return G=P1/P0 for positive prices.
Verify G=1+R for a stated price move.
Convert between gross return and simple return.
Update proportional wealth by W1=W0G when no other cash flows are stated.
Recover the price ratio from the wealth-growth factor without confusing it with P&L.

sessions.lesson: The gross return factor is G=P1/P0. Because R=(P1−P0)/P0, we have 1+R=P1/P0=G. If a position's wealth scales only with that price and there are no other cash flows or leverage complications, W1=W0G. Worked example: 100→110 gives G=1.10 and R=.10; 300 of proportional exposure becomes330. Guided check: 40→46 gives G=1.15; update 200 under the same simplified proportional assumption.

sessions.title: Multi-period compounding of simple returns
sessions.focus: Chain simple returns multiplicatively and distinguish compounded return from the arithmetic sum.
sessions.purpose: Adding period returns creates systematic errors whenever more than one nonzero return occurs.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute total simple return from a product of gross-return factors and expose the add-returns shortcut as invalid.
sessions.principalObstacle: Adding period percentages feels natural but ignores that each later return acts on a changed base.

Multiply period gross factors to obtain the total growth factor.

sessions.title: Log return & time additivity
sessions.focus: Define log return from a positive price ratio and derive its additive time aggregation.
sessions.purpose: Log-return additivity is useful later, but must be derived from logarithm laws rather than memorized as a slogan.
sessions.centralCapability: Use g=ln(P1/P0) and prove that consecutive log returns sum to ln(Pn/P0).
sessions.principalObstacle: Log-return additivity is memorized without deriving the cancellation of intermediate price ratios.
requiredOwnership: Represent a one-period log return as g=ln(P1/P0) for positive prices.
Compute exact one-period log returns as logarithmic expressions.
Add consecutive log returns using ln a+ln b=ln(ab).
Show intermediate prices cancel in the product of price ratios.
Distinguish log-return additivity from the non-additivity of simple returns.

sessions.lesson: For positive prices, the log return is g=ln(P1/P0). For P0→P1→P2, g1+g2=ln(P1/P0)+ln(P2/P1)=ln[(P1/P0)(P2/P1)]=ln(P2/P0). The middle price cancels. Worked example: 100→110→121 gives ln1.1+ln1.1=ln1.21. Guided check: 50→60→54 gives ln1.2+ln.9=ln1.08.

sessions.title: Simple ↔ log return conversion & domain
sessions.focus: Convert between return conventions while preserving the domain imposed by positive prices.
sessions.purpose: Treating log and simple returns as numerically identical or allowing impossible simple returns below −100% corrupts later analysis.
sessions.centralCapability: Use g=ln(1+R) and R=e^g−1 with R>−1 when prices are strictly positive.
sessions.principalObstacle: Simple and log returns are often treated as interchangeable numbers, and the −100% boundary is mishandled.
requiredOwnership: Use g=ln(1+R) as the simple-to-log conversion identity.
Convert a stated simple return to an exact log return.
Convert a stated log return to a simple return.
State the simple-return domain R>−1 for strictly positive endpoint prices.
Explain that simple and log returns are not generally numerically equal.

sessions.lesson: Since1+R=P1/P0, log return is g=ln(1+R). Inverting gives R=e^g−1. With strictly positive prices the ratio P1/P0 is positive, so R>−1; a −100% simple return corresponds to a zero endpoint price and has no finite log return. Worked example: R=.21 gives g=ln1.21; g=ln1.05 gives R=.05. Guided check: R=−.15 gives g=ln.85.

sessions.focus: Include an explicitly supplied per-unit cash distribution in a holding-period return without importing asset-pricing theory.
sessions.purpose: Ignoring cash distributions can make a losing price path look like a losing investment when total return is positive, or vice versa.
sessions.centralCapability: Compute price return and total simple return separately from P0,P1 and a stated cash distribution D.

sessions.focus: Compute simplified short price P&L without treating a price decline as a loss to the short.
sessions.purpose: Sign errors on shorts propagate into every later trading and backtest ledger.
sessions.centralCapability: Under an explicit simplified convention, short q units at P0 and cover at P1 has price P&L=q(P0−P1).
sessions.principalObstacle: Shorts reverse the price-P&L sign; learners often carry the long formula over without the signed-position logic.

sessions.lesson: In this simplified model, to short q>0 units means borrowed units are sold first at P0; to cover means buying those units back later at P1 to return them. Worked example: short10 at60 and cover55 gives+50; covering at65 gives−50. Guided check: short8 at25, cover23 gives+16. Real shorting can involve borrow fees, margin requirements and distributions owed; those are excluded unless explicitly supplied.

initialVersionAudit.policy: New M07 module: all fixed assessment obligations begin at version1; stable IDs are new and no historical M07 lesson/task exposure exists in the T22 Elite evidence store at authoring time. Later changes must version affected assessment or instruction contracts rather than recertify old evidence.

historicalLessonAnswerOverlap.rationale: Only old answer-bearing M07 lessons are mapped. Stable fixed-task IDs are retained. Existing evidence preceding the recorded lesson exposure remains historically eligible; later nominally independent attempts are contaminated. A newer clean lesson version never erases an older solved exposure during import/merge.

historicalGuidedPracticeOverlap.policy: Unsolved rehearsal is recorded separately and must not fabricate referenceSeenAt. Ordinary recorded lesson assistance remains. S03's former 80→92 guided check overlapped the S04 Main return subproblem without supplying the full fixed answer.

repairVersionAudit.policy: Stable IDs and chrono_t22_elite_course_evidence_v1 are retained. Materially changed prompt/evaluator contracts are obligationVersion2 and old attempts become stale under fingerprints. Narrowed ownership contracts generate new session contract hashes. Historical solved lesson exposure is timestamp-migrated; unsolved S03→S04 practice overlap is not promoted to a reveal. No old evidence is silently recertified.
